Brass-ringed pots stand ranked five deep on stepped iron tiers along the flank with foliage spilling over every edge; each pot carries one small white tag painted with a single green leaf and nothing else, and the tier fronts are plain smooth painted iron.

A sunken fern pit drops below the walkway, the whole bowl packed with fronds at every height and dripping stone at the back; the pots down there are unmarked red clay and the pit's brick edge is plain and mossy.
Wet iron grating runs over a warm bed so the plants come up through the slats in a green seam, steaming gently; small plain tin tags on wire stand among them, left bright and blank.
A benched propagating house: shallow seed pans set out in warm sand in perfect rows, each pan showing a different stage of green, each with a plain wooden stake pushed in at one corner.

A shallow lily pool holds its flat pads edge to edge with black water showing between them; the brick margin is plain and worn, and the one label in sight is a small enamel oval painted with a single blue flower.
A rockwork bank climbs the inner wall with alpines wedged into every crevice and water seeping darkly down the stone, the stone left bare and unlettered between the cushions of green.
A fruit wall of trained pears runs flat and fanned against warm brick, every branch tied with soft raffia to plain iron nails, and the fruits themselves hang in small muslin bags tied at the neck.
Hanging baskets go down the centre on brass chains at two heights, each one a shaggy ball of trailing stems, the chains hooked to plain rings and the baskets' rims wrapped in moss.
A whole cork-slab wall is bolted with epiphytes, roots gripping the cork in pale nets; small blank bark scraps hang on dyed red thread beside a few of them, and the cork between is plain and dry.

A potting corner heaped with work: dark peat in a plain timber bin, plain unmarked crates stacked to shoulder height, coarse sacking folded in a pile, and a bench of clean empty pots turned upside down.
A long stone trough of alpine cushions sits at hip height on brick piers, the trough face plain rough stone, the plants a mosaic of grey-green and silver studded with tiny flowers.
A stacked stone fernery in the corner drips from every ledge, small ferns rooted in the joints, and the water collects in a plain lead tray at its foot.
Vine rods are trained along wires just under the glass the whole length of the house, leaves flattened toward the light, each rod tied at intervals with twists of soft wire.
A bed of tender crowns stands under a row of bell glasses, each glass fogged inside and set on a plain saucer, the soil between them raked into neat dark ridges.
Climbing roses go up two of the iron ribs and out along the roof wires, flowers opening up there against the panes and a drift of fallen petals on the walkway below.
A dead tree trunk has been stood in the middle bed and clothed with moss and orchids, every fork holding a plant, the bark left bare and grey where nothing has taken.
A shallow warm tank of floating plants sits on brick piers at waist height, the surface a solid green skin with a hand-sized gap where something has just moved beneath it.
A row of citrus in plain wooden tubs stands along the sunny flank, fruit and flower on the same trees, the tub staves plain and silvered with age and banded in iron.
A bed of arums in black peat stands in ranks, every spathe turned slightly toward the glass, the peat surface dressed with clean grit.
A fig has been trained flat across the whole inner wall, its big lobed leaves overlapping like a green hide, the wall's brick showing plain between the branches.
Tiered staging steps up in five levels against the pier, every level packed rim to rim with small pots, and the whole face of it a wall of leaves with plain painted timber showing only at the ends.
A pineapple pit, sunk and warm, holds its spiked rosettes in dark soil under a low frame; the frame timbers are plain and tar-painted and the glass above them is misted from inside.
Tall canes and rush stand in a flooded corner bed with water lying visible between the stems, a plain plank duckboard laid across it to keep feet dry.
Bulbs are forced in plain earthenware pans on a high shelf, pale shoots leaning hard toward the light, each pan with a small tag painted with one round berry.
A wide sand bed holds squat succulents in plain clay pans arranged like a tiled floor, the sand raked smooth in curves between them and the pan rims left bare.

A copper tank fed by a thin pipe drips steadily into a bed of moisture-loving plants, the overflow channelled into a lead gutter running the length of the bench, moss filling every joint between the bricks beneath.
Shallow terracotta pans of moss are set directly on the damp floor in a grid, each pan a different shade of green from near-yellow to deep emerald, the clay rims darkened with moisture.
A central raised bed of dark soil holds standard roses in full leaf, each stem staked to a plain iron rod pushed deep, the bed edged in a low border of plain unmortared brick.
Carnation layers are pegged into open trays of sandy compost, each stem bent and pinned with a short bent wire, the whole tray set on a low iron shelf close to the warm floorpipes.
Staghorn ferns are bound to a flat panel of rough timber hung flat against the ironwork, each plant lashed on with strips of soft hessian, the fronds fanning outward in pale overlapping arcs.

A rank of tall palms in square wooden boxes occupies the central aisle, their trunks bare and fibrous for half their height before the fronds open, the box corners reinforced with plain iron strapping.
Cucumbers are trained up vertical strings from a warm bed, each plant reaching the roof wire and turned along it, young fruits hanging pale and downy at the leaf joints.
A low propagating frame sits on the warm floor with glass lights fogged from below, the frame timbers plain and painted dark, condensation running down the inside of every pane.
Maiden ferns in small red clay pots are packed tightly together on a dripping wet iron shelf, every frond touching its neighbour, the shelf supports dark with permanent damp.
A shallow channel cut in the floor brick runs with warm water the full width of the house, fed from a brass stopcock at one end, and aquatic cuttings float in it in loose bundles.
Melon plants are slung in small net hammocks of knotted twine from the roof wires, each swelling fruit cradled and hanging free, the stems tied back at the shoulder with a soft loop.
A wall of plain wooden shelves along the back runs floor to ceiling, every shelf holding earthenware crocks of dormant bulbs in dry sand, the shelves themselves unpainted and darkened with age.
Tomato plants are trained to a single rod each against the sunny glass, every side shoot pinched away, the rods tied at each truss to a horizontal wire with short loops of soft twine.
Moss is packed into the angles between the iron roof ribs where they meet the ridge, damp and dense, and small liverworts have spread themselves along the condensation seams below.
A warm dark corner holds a bark-lined box of bark chips where orchid roots run freely through the loose fill, the box sides plain unfinished timber held with iron tacks at the corners.
Flat grafting trays of newly joined stock and scion sit on a high warm shelf, each union wrapped in a strip of damp moss held with a winding of soft tape, the tape left plain.
A narrow bed of mint and warm-climate herbs runs along the base of the south-facing wall, the stems soft and crowded, the soil between them a dark mix of leaf mould and coarse sand.
A glass case set on iron legs at bench height holds a tight arrangement of small ferns and mosses under its lid, the inside surface of the glass misted with trapped humidity.
Pitcher plants hang in suspended wire baskets from a low cross-bar of iron, each dangling tube flushed red at the throat, the baskets packed with pale sphagnum holding the moisture in.
Dense rows of pricked-out seedlings fill a long shallow box of fine compost on the main bench, every seedling standing separate in its own small hole, the surface levelled flat.
Forced chicory crowns pack a deep box of sand under the main bench, pale blanched shoots pushing up through the sand in a dense cream flush, the box sides plain unfinished deal.
Wax begonias in plain round clay pots stand in a close block on the lower tier, every plant the same height, the tier surface dressed with a layer of clean ash to keep the moisture even.
Passion flower stems are looped through a grid of plain iron wire stretched across the back window, each stem secured at every crossing with a twist of soft lead wire, leaves pressed to the glass.
Cut sweet peas fill a plain iron bucket in the potting corner, the stems long and the flowers loose, a string handle on the bucket and the inside of it already stained green from water.

Tender perennial cuttings are stood in plain jam-jar sized glass tubes of water along a low bracket shelf, roots just visible as white threads in the clear water, the shelf fixed with plain iron brackets.

A cold frame bank of six low lights runs along the base of the north wall, each sash propped on a clay pot at different heights, the seedlings inside packed tight and the timber frames swollen and dark with moisture.
Moss has been laid in thick mats over a whole raised bed and pinned flat with short split canes, the surface a close green carpet with small fern fronds beginning to push through at the edges.

Pelargoniums crowd a long slate shelf, their pots touching, the stems leggy and leaning at angles against the glass, and a scatter of fallen florets rests on the slate between them in pale pink drifts.
Iron pipes run just above soil level across the floor bed, wrapped in cloth at the joints and warm to the air above them, the soil between banked up in low ridges over the pipes.
A whole gable end is given to staghorn ferns mounted on rough timber boards bolted to the brickwork, each plant spreading its flat antler fronds outward, the boards darkened with moisture and age.
A double row of standard fuchsias stands on the central staging, each trained to a single straight stem tied to a plain rod, the flowering heads at uniform height and the stems bare below.
Sweet peas have been taken up the full height of the rear wall on a frame of cane and tarred twine, the stems twisted loosely at each horizontal, the flowers opening from the base upward.
A lead cistern in the corner holds water at soil level, broad-leafed aquatics rooted in sand at the bottom, the lead sides greened over and the surface broken only by a single open flower.
A bank of deep cold shelves is stacked with dormant tubers laid in dry sand in plain timber trays, each tray slid in close above the next, the whole bank filling the shadowed alcove.
Cucumbers run up the sunny side on vertical wires pegged to the glass frame, the large leaves pressing flat to the pane and the young fruits hanging straight and pale among them.
A plain lead gutter fixed along the ridge collects the drip from the glass and feeds it down a chain into a half-barrel below, the barrel brimming and the chain dark and mossy at its lower end.
Shallow earthenware pans of moss and liverwort cover the whole of one lower staging shelf, the surface uneven and soft, each pan with a different green texture from its neighbour.
A warm corner holds a heap of fresh coco-fibre piled high against the brick, and the potting barrow beside it is loaded with filled plain pots, the soil dark and mounded over each rim.
Camellias in large plain clay pots stand at the entrance end, the pots raised on plain brick feet, every bud closed and the foliage a deep uniform gloss under the bright glass above.
Waxed cloth has been laid in strips over a whole cold bench and weighted at the edges with clay pots turned on their sides, the cloth bellying slightly over the seedlings warming underneath.
Maidenhair fern fills a tiered wire stand in the damp corner beside the water pipe, each tier a solid curtain of fine fronds, the wire dark with rust and the whole stand trembling with drip.
A row of half-barrels along the south wall holds specimen palms, the trunks ringed with old leaf scars, the fronds arching out over the walkway and the barrel staves broad and iron-banded.

Aquilegia seedlings stand in a shallow tray of wet sand on the upper shelf, each in its own small plain pot, the whole tray tilted very slightly toward the glass and the seedlings all leaning the same way.
A thick rope of trained wisteria runs the length of the main beam under the ridge, the old stems twisted together as thick as a wrist, the young growth hanging in long pale catkins below.
The floor of the corner bay is sunk and filled with coarse gravel, and bromeliads are set directly into the gravel in a close mass, their cups each holding a pool of standing water.
Tender bulbs are stored dry in open-weave baskets on the topmost shelf, the baskets stacked two high, the papery bulb skins showing through the weave and the shelf above them dark with warmth.
A pair of bay trees clipped into tight columns stand on either side of the main path junction, their pots sunk into plain square timber boxes, the clipped surfaces dense and even.
Passiflora has run across the full length of the upper wires on the west side, the stems cabling back on themselves where they have outrun the wire, the tendrils still reaching into the open air.

A low propagating frame of brick and slate sits in the warmest bay, its slate lid propped on a wedge of wood, the interior steaming and the cuttings inside showing their first pale roots through the glass side.
Terracotta long toms hold tall amaryllis in flower along the highest shelf, each stem straight and bare to a heavy head, the pots thin and dark red against the bright sky beyond the glass.
A long shallow trough of cut moss peat runs the length of the back wall with carnivorous plants set into it at intervals, each rosette low and open, the peat surface kept dark and wet between them.

Warm pipes run along the base of the south wall and ferns have been pressed into the crevices above them, their fronds arching out over the path in overlapping layers, the brickwork behind plain and lime-washed.

Espaliered camellias cover the end wall, each branch fanned in a perfect herringbone against the glass, the dark leaves pressing up toward the panes and a scatter of fallen blooms lying on the sill below.
Small orchid pans hang in a tiered wooden frame on gut strings at three heights, every pan a different species, the roots trailing through the mesh of the base in pale loops.
A gravel bed of dwarf bulbs fills the whole centre section, each clump in full flower at a different height, the gravel between them raked flat and the bed edged in plain tarred board.
A specimen palm stands free in its own bed of dark loam, the trunk ringed with old growth scars, fronds fanning out to touch the glass on three sides and the loam surface topped with coarse bark.
Wire columns wrapped in wet sphagnum rise from the floor bed at intervals, climbing aroids anchored to each one with soft copper ties, the roots vanishing into the moss.
A shallow copper tray on plain iron legs holds a single specimen water lily in full bloom, its round leaves resting on still water, the tray edge plain and green with oxidation.
Cut bamboo poles are lashed in a grid just under the roof glass, and climbing plants have been wound onto every stem, the whole ceiling a dense woven green with small gaps of pale sky above.
A raised hotbed of fresh manure under pine boards holds melon seedlings in individual clay pots sunk to their rims, each stem pinched to one leader and tied loosely to a short cane.
Pitcher plants fill a slatted cedar case packed with living sphagnum, the pitchers hanging at different angles, some still sealed and pale, others open and dark at the throat.
A succession bed of dwarf dahlias in dark loam steps down in three terraces, each terrace at a different stage of bud and flower, the loam faces plain and tamped smooth.
An iron forcing frame sunk into the floor holds crowns of rhubarb in total darkness, the lid propped just clear on a brick at one end so a crack of warm air moves through.
Pelargoniums in plain clay pots line every rung of a tall iron ladder leant against the pier, the pots balanced on each step in a column of red and pink that reaches the roof wire.
A bed of tree ferns stands in the wet corner, trunks rough and fibrous with old frond scars, the canopy closing overhead and the soil below kept black and glistening with moisture.
Staghorn ferns are mounted on plain timber boards hung flat against the warm wall, each plant spreading from a dry brown base into wide antler fronds that cast shadow on the board beneath.

A long iron bench holds cuttings jars of clear water in a dense row, each jar holding stems at different stages of rooting, the pale roots visible through the glass and the bench surface plain and wet.
Cape bulbs in fine silver sand fill a plain wooden flat set close under the glass, each bulb showing its tip above the surface, the sand pressed firm and the flat edge plain sawn timber.
Climbing passion flowers have taken every roof wire on the north quarter, the stems crossing and recrossing in a dense lattice and the flowers hanging between the panes in clusters of blue and white.
A pair of standard bay trees in iron-hooped tubs flank the inner door, clipped to dense drums on clear stems, the tub iron plain black and the soil surface covered in wet gravel.
A warm floor bed of cannas stands in heavy dark loam, the paddle leaves overlapping at every angle and the flower spikes standing clear of the foliage, the bed edge a plain row of brick set on edge.

Dried seed heads on long wire stems are stood in a plain earthenware crock in the corner, gathered from the house's own plants, the papery heads catching the glass light and casting fine shadows on the wall.
A raised peat block wall has been built along the shaded pier and planted through with ferns and small primulas in every joint, the peat face dark and damp and the plants pushing out at all angles.

Chrysanthemums in large plain earthenware pots are staked to single canes with soft twine at three heights, the blooms all turned the same way toward the south glass, the pot surfaces plain and terracotta-red.
A tank of tropical lilies sunk to floor level holds its broad leaves above the rim, the stems visible as pale columns in the dark water and one flower open at the surface, its petals spread flat.
